The group helper starts an inert direct-child anchor in the owned group and retains that child's unreaped PID until every other member is observed absent. The Rust test parent is separately polled/reaped. Cleanup observes group membership independently of parent EOF on normal completion, early failure, timeout, spawn failure and pipe error; surviving descendants receive bounded TERM then KILL handling. The anchor remains reserved across those signals, including when killed, so the cleanup does not signal a reused group ID. It never uses a zombie getpgid response as proof that the reservation was lost. Once no application members remain, closing the control pipe causes the anchor to kill its own group, and the owner waits for the anchor before confirming cleanup.

Failed observation or custody does not become a successful empty-group result. The runner records parent and group outcomes separately, stays BLOCKED, and retains the private fixture directory and Mongo container if process cleanup is unconfirmed. It disposes dependent resources only after confirmation; sanitized partial output and the fixed failure phase remain. The 120-second test deadline is unchanged. TERM/KILL waits each have a ten-second budget, with bounded process observations; this is cleanup control, not a measured application shutdown or recovery guarantee.

This reasoning applies to the documented single-threaded POSIX owner with default SIGCHLD behavior and exclusive custody of waiting for the anchor. The inspected Rust gateway fixture inherits the process group and does not daemonize. The helper is not containment for arbitrary executables that deliberately leave the group, and its receipt cannot cover such an expanded workload without a new custody design. No reliance on Rust destructors after external SIGTERM remains in the cleanup proof.

`LocalCluster.removePod` now puts the exact validated Pod UID into `DeleteOptions.preconditions.uid` on the raw API DELETE request, with zero grace. The new command transport writes that JSON to stdin. A name replacement produces server refusal; there is no name-only fallback or retry. The original context, local-server, namespace-identity, Pod-label and resource restrictions remain, and `processDeathObserved` stays false. This closes the source race; a future actual fault still requires its separately authorized scope and independent process-death observation.
